opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one people sometimes gloss over because these models are so impressive. Vanilla vision-language models bring something genuinely valuable: a lot of world knowledge and common-sense semantic understanding that you'd never collect purely from driving data. If you see something unusual, like a person in a costume or debris of an odd shape, a VLM has a decent prior on what it is and how it might behave. That's real.

But there are several gaps when you hold them up against what a driving system actually has to do.

The first is the sensors. Most VLMs are built around camera images, often single frames or short clips at fairly low resolution. A production autonomous vehicle uses multiple cameras, lidar, and radar, all calibrated together, and it has to reason in 3D with metric precision. Knowing that "there's a cyclist on the left" isn't enough. You need to know where that cyclist is to within tens of centimeters, how fast they're moving, and what their heading is. Language-centric models aren't naturally good at that kind of precise spatial and geometric reasoning, and you can't just bolt lidar onto them without significant work.

The second is time and dynamics. Driving is fundamentally about predicting how a scene evolves, multiple agents interacting with each other, over several seconds. VLMs mostly do static, or loosely temporal, understanding. They aren't natively built to produce well-calibrated multimodal predictions of future trajectories, or to plan a smooth, physically feasible trajectory for the vehicle itself.

Third, there's latency and compute. A car has to make decisions many times per second on onboard hardware. A large VLM with billions of parameters, autoregressively decoding tokens, is a hard fit for those real-time, power-constrained conditions. So in practice you end up distilling, or using these big models offboard as teachers, labelers, or for data mining, rather than running them directly in the loop.

Fourth, and probably the most important, is reliability and verifiability. The bar for safety here is extremely high. VLMs hallucinate, and their failure modes are hard to characterize. In driving, you need to be able to measure performance rigorously, validate it in simulation over enormous numbers of scenarios, understand the long tail, and have some structure you can reason about. A system that's right 99% of the time and confidently wrong the rest of the time is not acceptable. That's why I think a lot of the value comes from combining the semantic richness of these foundation models with structured intermediate representations, things like objects, maps, and trajectories, that you can inspect, supervise, and verify.

So my view is that they're a very powerful ingredient, especially for long-tail semantic understanding and for scaling up the data engine, but a vanilla VLM on its own doesn't meet the bar. You need to adapt it to the sensor suite, ground it in 3D and in time, make it efficient enough to run onboard, and embed it in a system you can actually validate to the standards that putting cars on public roads requires.

r001.rationale: The response says vanilla VLMs are mostly camera-based and lack integrated lidar/radar reasoning for calibrated, precise 3D awareness.

r002.rationale: It says driving requires predicting scene evolution and agent interactions over several seconds.

r003.rationale: It mentions unusual objects, but does not identify unfamiliar input domains as causing erroneous VLM predictions.

r004.rationale: It recommends structured representations and validation, but does not state that stack design mitigates ML errors from inputs outside the training distribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So, I think vision-language models are a very exciting foundation, and we've been doing a lot of work building on them. But when you take one off the shelf and ask whether it can drive a car, there are several places where it just doesn't meet the bar.

The first one is the sensing and 3D understanding. These models are trained mostly on internet images and text, so they're very good at semantics, at telling you what's in a scene and reasoning about it in language. But driving is fundamentally a 3D, metric problem. You need to know precisely where things are, how fast they're moving, where they'll be in two or three seconds. And a vehicle like ours has cameras, lidar, radar, all of them fused over time. A vanilla VLM doesn't natively consume that. It's not trained on it, it doesn't have strong geometric priors, and it tends to be fairly weak at fine-grained spatial reasoning, like estimating distances or velocities. So you need to extend it, both in the inputs it takes and in what it's been trained to represent.

The second is the long tail. These models learn the common case very well, but their internet-scale training data is quite different from the distribution a car actually sees. The things that matter most for safety are rare: unusual construction zones, emergency vehicles behaving in unexpected ways, a pedestrian doing something strange. The model needs to be robust and calibrated in exactly those situations, and that doesn't come for free from generic web data. You need large amounts of real driving data and targeted data for the rare cases, and you need to be able to measure performance on those very carefully.

Then there's the output side. A VLM produces text, essentially. Driving requires precise, continuous actions: a trajectory, with constraints around comfort and safety, produced consistently frame after frame. So you have to teach the model to produce those outputs, and you have to think hard about how it interfaces with the rest of the system.

The fourth piece is latency and compute. A big VLM is great in a data center, but on the vehicle you have hard real-time constraints and limited power. So there's a lot of work in distillation, in making the models efficient, in deciding what runs on board versus what you use offboard for things like data mining, auto-labeling and simulation. Actually, that offboard setting is where the large models shine most immediately, because you're not bound by those constraints.

And finally, and maybe most importantly, there's verification. In driving, it's not enough for the model to be right most of the time. You need to be able to validate that the system as a whole is safe before you deploy it, and that's hard to do with a monolithic black box that reasons in free-form language. So you need structure, redundancy, and a serious evaluation and simulation infrastructure around it.

So to summarize, I see VLMs as a very strong prior, world knowledge and reasoning that you'd otherwise have to learn from scratch. But getting from that to a driver requires grounding them in 3D and in sensors, training them on the right driving data, giving them the right output interface, making them efficient, and wrapping them in a system you can actually verify.

r003.rationale: It says generic internet training data differs from the distribution cars encounter and that rare driving situations require targeted data for robustness and calibration, conveying that unfamiliar domains can undermine predictions.

astra-6.text:
I think vision-language models are very impressive at describing what’s in a scene and bringing broad semantic knowledge to it. But there’s a substantial gap between describing a scene and driving safely through it.

For driving, you need very precise spatial and temporal understanding. Where exactly is that pedestrian? How fast are they moving? Are they about to step into the road? A model can give you a plausible description of an image while missing a detail that completely changes what the vehicle should do.

You also need to reason over time and connect perception to actions. The world responds to what you do, so it’s not enough to answer a question about a static image. You need to anticipate how a situation could evolve under different actions, make a decision, and keep updating that decision as new observations arrive.

And then there’s reliability. You need to operate in real time, understand uncertainty, and handle unusual situations consistently. Broad knowledge is incredibly useful, but a fluent answer doesn’t by itself tell you that the model has understood the scene accurately enough to control a vehicle. So I see these models as a powerful foundation, but they need additional capabilities and training grounded in the driving task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision-language models are very powerful at capturing semantic information about the world. They can look at a scene and describe what’s happening, and that’s useful. But for autonomous driving, describing the scene is only part of the problem. You need to understand precisely where things are, how they’re moving, and how they might interact with you over time.

A model might tell you there’s a cyclist next to the road, but we need to know whether that cyclist is going to enter our path, when that might happen, and what action we should take. That requires spatial and temporal understanding, as well as an understanding of how our own actions affect the situation.

Then there’s reliability. A plausible answer isn’t enough when you’re controlling a vehicle. You need the system to handle uncertainty and perform consistently across a very broad range of situations. So I see these models as providing valuable capabilities, but those capabilities need to be grounded in perception, prediction, and planning before they can meet the requirements of driving.
